warmup.q: A builder processor's test checks two things: the compile succeeds, and the generated text contains class LampBuilder. A bug makes the processor drop the ? from shade: String?, so the builder has shade(shade: String). What does the test do?
options: It fails: the generated code doesn't compile
It passes: the builder compiles and still contains class LampBuilder
It fails: KSP reports an error for the nullable parameter
It passes only when Lamp is a data class
warmup.why: A builder with a non-null shade is valid Kotlin, so the compile succeeds and the text check finds its class. Nothing fails until someone calls shade(null). Section 2 runs exactly this bug through all four checks: a golden file and one call into the code catch it.

opening:
Before moving day, a careful family does a practice pack. One empty room, a few boxes, the helper with the clipboard, and a good look at the cards the helper writes. If the lamp gets the wrong card, they want to find out today, in that room, not at the new house with the van gone.

Since the first lab of this track, you've run tests that someone else wrote: a few lines of Kotlin compiled in memory, then checks on what came out. Lesson 7 ended on their limit, because they never run a second, incremental build. Now you'll write that kind of test yourself, the way the author of a processor library does. The trap is a test that looks thorough and checks almost nothing: it passes, the processor is broken, and a lamp with no shade fails on a user's machine.

In this lesson, we'll build a small test bench of our own, make the four checks every processor test makes, keep golden files, pin errors to their file and line, and name what an in-memory test can't see. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a practice pack in an empty room and a lamp with no shade. The bench compiled a few lines in memory, and four checks looked at the result: the exit code and a contains passed a broken builder, while a golden file and one call with null caught it. Errors came back as a file, a line and a text, and the real build covered what the room couldn't.

In a processor test of your own, find each test that stops at exitCode or contains, and add a call into the generated code.

Next, we'll step back and choose. When is reflection good enough, when does a job need a compiler plugin, and when is kapt still the only helper there is?

sections.h: A practice pack in an empty room: compiling a few lines in memory
sections.html:
A processor test needs four things. It needs a few lines of source code, and KSP to run the processor on them. It needs the Kotlin compiler, to compile the sources together with whatever was generated. And it needs a way to look at the results. A real Gradle build does all four, and takes seconds and a whole project per test. So processor tests run the compiler in memory instead, inside the test's own JVM.

The library that does it here is kctfork, a community fork of Kotlin Compile Testing. It runs KSP2 and the Kotlin compiler on source code held in strings, in a fresh folder per compile, and hands back what happened. Its Maven group, the first part of the name a build uses to download it, is dev.zacsweers.kctfork, and its classes still live in the old package, com.tschuchort.compiletesting. Java has had annotation processors, programs that javac runs while it compiles, since Java 6, and KSP is Kotlin's own way to do that job for Kotlin code. Java's processors have a test library of the same kind, Google's compile-testing, and kctfork describes itself as "in the spirit of" it.

Every test that calls kctfork by hand repeats the same dozen lines. A test harness is the reusable code around a test that does the setting up, the running and the collecting, so that each test states only what's special about it. This lesson's lab is one, ProcessorBench, and its tests use it on two processors from earlier lessons:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: Google's compile-testing runs javac with your processor, in memory
JavaFileObject lamp = JavaFileObjects.forSourceString("movemate.Lamp", """
        package movemate;

        @Builder
        public class Lamp { ... }
        """);
Compilation compilation = Compiler.javac()
        .withProcessors(new BuilderProcessor())    // passed directly: no services file
        .compile(lamp);
Kotlin
val bench = ProcessorBench(KctforkCompiler)      // kctfork, plugged in from src/test
val run = bench.run(
    Source(
        "Lamp.kt",
        """
        package movemate

        import workbench.ksp.annotations.Builder

        @Builder
        data class Lamp(val name: String, val bulbs: Int, val shade: String?)
        """,
    ),
    processors = listOf(BuilderProcessorProvider()), // passed directly: no services file
)

Both versions hand the processor over directly, so the services file from lesson 2 plays no part in a test. The bench does one quiet favour first: it trims each source's indent. Then line 1 is the package line, and a message's line number matches what you count in the test.

The result carries what the four checks need. One part is a class loader, the JVM object that finds compiled classes and loads them into the running program. kctfork's class loader sees your source classes and the generated ones, and that's how a test can call LampBuilder although the test itself was compiled long before LampBuilder existed.

You may wonder why the compiler is a parameter of the bench. The plain reason is the build: kctfork is on this project's test and demo class paths only, and the bench lives in src/main, so it can't create a kctfork compile itself. Instead the bench asks for the one thing it needs, any InMemoryCompiler, and the tests hand it one. Giving an object what it needs, instead of letting it build its own, is called dependency injection, and this is it in miniature; the capstone after this track builds it at full size. That split pays for itself: the bench's message parsing and golden files are tested with no compiler at all, in milliseconds. A compile costs more. The first one in a test JVM takes 4 to 7 seconds while the compiler loads, and later ones under a second.

In the picture, this is the practice pack: a few boxes in an empty room, the same helper, and a look at the cards. The picture breaks in one useful place. kctfork tidies the room after every practice pack, deleting its caches, so it never sees a second build. A compile that ran tells you almost nothing yet, though. The checks do the work.

sections.h: Four checks, weakest first: a builder bug that two of them miss
sections.html:
Every processor test makes some of four checks. The exit code says how the compile ended: OK, COMPILATION_ERROR when a processor called logger.error or the code didn't compile, or INTERNAL_ERROR when a processor threw. The generated text is what the processor wrote. The messages are what it and the compiler printed. Last, calling the generated code runs it through the class loader. Which of them does a test really need? Let's plant a bug and find out.

The lab's builder processor turns each parameter's type into KotlinPoet's TypeName through one function, and the demo passes it a broken one that drops the question mark: typeOf = { it.toTypeName().copy(nullable = false) }. For Lamp, that turns shade(shade: String?) into shade(shade: String). WeakTestsDemo runs that builder through the four checks, weakest first:

check 1, the exit code is OK:            passes   (OK)
check 2, the text contains LampBuilder:  passes
check 3, the golden file:                FAILS at line 18
    expected: public fun shade(shade: String?): LampBuilder = apply { this.shade = shade }
    actual:   public fun shade(shade: String): LampBuilder = apply { this.shade = shade }
check 4, call shade(null):               FAILS with NullPointerException: Parameter specified as non-null is null: method movemate.LampBuilder.shade, parameter shade

The first two checks pass, and they pass honestly: the broken builder compiles, and it does contain class LampBuilder. A test made of those two proves that the processor didn't crash. The bug would reach the first family whose lamp has no shade.

The third check is a golden file: a stored copy of the output you expect, compared with the real output on every run, with a way to rewrite it on purpose. The bench's checkGolden writes a missing golden file and fails once, so a person reads the new text before it becomes the standard. It reports the first line that differs, counting from 1, and UPDATE_GOLDEN=true ./gradlew :ksp:test ... rewrites every file it checks. A golden file is a proofreader with no sense of proportion: it flags a moved space as loudly as a lost question mark. A KotlinPoet upgrade that changes how it formats code will fail every golden file you have, as KotlinPoet 2.4.0 did when it changed how annotation arrays are written.

The fourth check calls shade(null) through the class loader and gets the generated code's own exception. That one checks behaviour, and formatting can't fool it. Here are the four checks in one test, for KSP and for javac:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: the same checks with compile-testing and Truth
Compilation compilation = javac().withProcessors(new BuilderProcessor()).compile(lamp);
assertThat(compilation).succeededWithoutWarnings();                      // 1 and 3
assertThat(compilation).generatedSourceFile("movemate.LampBuilder")      // 2, against a stored file
        .hasSourceEquivalentTo(JavaFileObjects.forResource("golden/LampBuilder.java"));
// 4: compile-testing's checks stop at the compile; call the generated builder
//    from a test in a module whose own build runs the processor
Kotlin
val run = bench.run(lamp, processors = listOf(BuilderProcessorProvider()))
assertThat(run.exitCode).isEqualTo("OK")                                         // 1. the exit code
assertMatchesGolden(run.generated("movemate/LampBuilder.kt"),                    // 2. the text
    goldenDir.resolve("LampBuilder.kt.golden"))
assertThat(run.messages).isEmpty()                                               // 3. the messages
val builder = run.newInstance("movemate.LampBuilder")                            // 4. call the code
run.call(builder, "name", "desk lamp")
run.call(builder, "bulbs", 1)
run.call(builder, "shade", null)
assertThat(run.call(builder, "build").toString()).isEqualTo("Lamp(name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null)")

A test that only compiles proves the processor didn't crash. Call the code it wrote.

Pair each golden file with at least one call into the generated code. The golden file catches any change; the call tells you whether the change matters. The two tests left are the unhappy ones, the inputs your processor must refuse.

steps: Run WeakTestsDemo and read the four verdicts. Which two would a quick test have stopped at?
In WeakTestsDemo.kt, change copy(nullable = false) to copy(), so the builder keeps its question marks. Predict the four verdicts, then run it again.

code.title: WeakTestsDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.ksp.l08.demo import com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.SymbolProcessorProvider import com.squareup.kotlinpoet.ksp.toTypeName import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.KotlinCompilation import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.SourceFile import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.configureKsp import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.kspSourcesDir import java.io.File import java.io.OutputStream import workbench.ksp.l08.BuilderProcessor import workbench.ksp.l08.Compiled import workbench.ksp.l08.GoldenResult import workbench.ksp.l08.InMemoryCompiler import workbench.ksp.l08.ProcessorBench import workbench.ksp.l08.Source import workbench.ksp.l08.checkGolden // A builder processor with one planted bug: it drops the '?' from every parameter type, so shade(shade: String?) // comes out as shade(shade: String). Then the four checks, weakest first. Which ones notice? // Uses the reference bench; add -Pmine=l08 for yours. // ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l08.demo.WeakTestsDemoKt fun main() { val buggy = SymbolProcessorProvider { env -> BuilderProcessor(env.codeGenerator, env.logger, typeOf = { it.toTypeName().copy(nullable = false) }) } val lamp = Source( "Lamp.kt", """ package movemate import workbench.ksp.annotations.Builder @Builder data class Lamp(val name: String, val bulbs: Int, val shade: String?) """, ) val run = ProcessorBench(DemoCompiler).run(lamp, processors = listOf(buggy)) val text = run.generated("movemate/LampBuilder.kt") println("check 1, the exit code is OK: ${verdict(run.exitCode == "OK")} (${run.exitCode})") println("check 2, the text contains LampBuilder: ${verdict("class LampBuilder" in text)}") val golden = File("src/test/resources/workbench/ksp/l08/golden/LampBuilder.kt.golden") when (val g = checkGolden(text, golden, update = false)) { is GoldenResult.Differs -> { println("check 3, the golden file: FAILS at line ${g.line}") println(" expected: ${g.expected.trim()}") println(" actual: ${g.actual.trim()}") } else -> println("check 3, the golden file: $g") } val builder = run.newInstance("movemate.LampBuilder") run.call(builder, "name", "desk lamp") run.call(builder, "bulbs", 1) try { run.call(builder, "shade", null) println("check 4, call shade(null): passes") } catch (e: NullPointerException) { println("check 4, call shade(null): FAILS with ${e.javaClass.simpleName}: ${e.message}") } } private fun verdict(ok: Boolean) = if (ok) "passes" else "FAILS " /** The demo's own copy of the bench's compiler (the tests' copy lives in src/test, which demos can't see). */ private object DemoCompiler : InMemoryCompiler { override fun compile(sources: List<Source>, processors: List<SymbolProcessorProvider>, options: Map<String, String>): Compiled { val compilation = KotlinCompilation().apply { workingDir = File("build/kctfork/demo/l08").apply { deleteRecursively() } this.sources = sources.map { SourceFile.kotlin(it.fileName, it.text, trimIndent = false) } inheritClassPath = true jvmTarget = "21" messageOutputStream = OutputStream.nullOutputStream() configureKsp { symbolProcessorProviders += processors processorOptions += options } } val result = compilation.compile() return Compiled(result.exitCode.name, result.messages, compilation.kspSourcesDir.resolve("kotlin"), result.classLoader) } }

try.expect: With the bug, checks 1 and 2 pass, check 3 fails at line 18 with shade(shade: String?) expected and shade(shade: String) actual, and check 4 fails with NullPointerException: Parameter specified as non-null is null: method movemate.LampBuilder.shade, parameter shade. With copy(), checks 1, 2 and 4 pass, and check 3 prints Matches.

sections.h: Errors by file and line: pinning down what the processor refuses
sections.html:
Lesson 5 taught the builder to refuse bad input with an error on the exact box. A test of that has three things to pin down: the compile failed, the message says the right thing, and it points at the right file and line. The last part is the one people skip, and it's the one users feel.

Here is what kctfork printed for @Builder interface Shape, with the interface on line 6:

e: Error occurred in KSP, check log for detail
e: [ksp] /…/sources/Shape.kt:6: @Builder goes on a class, but Shape is an interface

And here is the Kotlin compiler on a user's file that passes an Int to shade:

e: file:///…/sources/Use.kt:5:16 Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Int', but 'String?' was expected.

Three shapes of message, then. KSP's own has [ksp], an absolute path, a line and no column. The compiler's has file://, a line and a column. And a line with no location at all, like kctfork's summary Error occurred in KSP. The paths point into a temporary folder that changes with every run, so a test must never compare them. The bench's parseMessage splits each line into a Message: the severity, the file name only, the line and the text. It skips lines that aren't messages, such as a stack trace. Then a test can say exactly what it means:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: compile-testing finds an error by its text, file and line
assertThat(compilation).failed();
assertThat(compilation).hadErrorContaining("@Builder goes on a class, but Shape is an interface")
        .inFile(bad)
        .onLine(6);
Kotlin
assertThat(run.exitCode).isEqualTo("COMPILATION_ERROR")
assertThat(run.errors).contains(
    Message('e', "Bad.kt", 6, "@Builder goes on a class, but Shape is an interface"),
    Message('e', "Bad.kt", 9, "@Builder goes on a class, but Van is an object"),
    Message('e', "Bad.kt", 12, "SafeBuilder can't call Safe's private constructor. Make the constructor public or internal."),
)

That Kotlin test compiles one file with three bad classes and expects three errors in one build, each on its own line. The lines are 6, 9 and 12, the lines of interface Shape, object Van and class Safe, not the lines of their @Builder notes. KSP reports a declaration's own line, and so does javac, which is why compile-testing's onLine(6) finds the same line. Count from the package line, which is line 1 because the bench trimmed the indent.

An error test checks the text and the line. A message on the wrong line is a bug the user feels.

In the picture, the helper's note must say which box, not "somewhere in the hall". The same note in a real build points at your real file. The practice room, though, can't show everything about moving day.

sections.h: What a practice pack can't show: the real build, TestKit and debugging
sections.html:
An in-memory test is fast because it skips the build, and so it can't see anything that lives in the build. Lesson 7's bugs are the clearest case. kctfork deletes its caches and runs a clean pass on every compile, so a wrong Dependencies passes every kctfork test you can write. The services file is another: tests hand the provider over directly, so a missing services file passes them all, and the real build then fails with e: [ksp] No providers found in processor classpath. Options come through the real build too, and lesson 7 showed that a new value reaches the processor only when it's a tracked input of the task. And a multiplatform project's per-target KSP tasks exist only in Gradle.

For those, there's Gradle TestKit: Gradle's own library for running a real build from a test. In the Gradle docs' words, "builds run in a separate process from your tests". A TestKit test writes a tiny project to a folder, runs Gradle on it, and checks the tasks and the files:

Java
// A TestKit test, sketched (this lab has no TestKit dependency)
BuildResult result = GradleRunner.create()
        .withProjectDir(projectDir)               // a tiny build the test writes on disk
        .withArguments("compileKotlin", "-Pksp.incremental.log=true")
        .build();
assertEquals(TaskOutcome.SUCCESS, result.task(":kspKotlin").getOutcome());
Kotlin
// A TestKit test, sketched (this lab has no TestKit dependency)
val result = GradleRunner.create()
    .withProjectDir(projectDir)                   // a tiny build the test writes on disk
    .withArguments("compileKotlin", "-Pksp.incremental.log=true")
    .build()
assertThat(result.task(":kspKotlin")?.outcome).isEqualTo(TaskOutcome.SUCCESS)

Each such test costs a Gradle daemon and a real KSP run: seconds, where kctfork costs a fraction of one. So a library keeps a handful of them, for the services file, one edit-and-rebuild for each aggregating output, and the options. This course's lab has no TestKit dependency. The playground in labs/ksp/app plays that part by hand, as lesson 7's Try-its did.

When a test fails and you don't know why, debug in this order. First, read the generated file: the kctfork work folder keeps it, under ksp/sources/kotlin/, and most surprises are visible there. Second, add a temporary logger.warn("..."): a warning shows at Gradle's default log level, and logger.info only with --info. Third, a debugger. A kctfork test is an ordinary JUnit test, so debug it like one. In a real build, KSP2 runs inside the Gradle daemon, so KSP's docs suggest starting Gradle with -Dorg.gradle.debug=true and attaching to it.

Test a processor's logic in memory, and its wiring in a real build.

In the picture, the practice pack checks the helper's cards; only moving day checks that the van turns up. Together they cover the move.

java.html: // Closest Java equivalent: Google's compile-testing with Truth import static com.google.testing.compile.CompilationSubject.assertThat; import static com.google.testing.compile.Compiler.javac; class BuilderProcessorTest { @Test void reportsAnInterfaceOnItsOwnLine() { JavaFileObject bad = JavaFileObjects.forSourceString("movemate.Shape", """ package movemate; import movemate.annotations.Builder; @Builder interface Shape {} """); Compilation compilation = javac().withProcessors(new BuilderProcessor()).compile(bad); assertThat(compilation).failed(); // 1. the outcome assertThat(compilation) .hadErrorContaining("@Builder goes on a class, but Shape is an interface") // 3. the text .inFile(bad) .onLine(6); // and the line // 2 and 4: generatedSourceFile(...) for the text; calling the code is not among its checks } }

kotlin.title: BuilderProcessorTest.kt
kotlin.html: class BuilderProcessorTest { private val bench = ProcessorBench(KctforkCompiler) @Test fun `reports an interface on its own line`() { val run = bench.run( Source( "Shape.kt", """ package movemate import workbench.ksp.annotations.Builder @Builder interface Shape """, ), processors = listOf(BuilderProcessorProvider()), ) assertThat(run.exitCode).isEqualTo("COMPILATION_ERROR") // 1. the outcome assertThat(run.errors) // 3. text and line .contains(Message('e', "Shape.kt", 6, "@Builder goes on a class, but Shape is an interface")) assertThat(run.generated).isEmpty() // 2. nothing written } }

compare.note: The two tests have the same shape: source in a string, the processor passed directly, then the outcome, the text and the line. compile-testing came first and kctfork follows its spirit. The differences are in the details. compile-testing works through Truth subjects (failed(), hadErrorContaining(...).inFile(...).onLine(...)), while the bench parses messages into plain Message values that any assertion library can compare. Both report the declaration's line, 6 here, not the annotation's. And the kctfork result carries a class loader, so a Kotlin test can call the generated code in the same test, the fourth check; compile-testing's documented checks stop at the compile.

worked.title: Turn a bug report into a test that fails first

steps.say: The report: "The builder breaks for my class with a private constructor: the build fails, but the message points at line 1." Before touching the processor, reproduce it on the bench, with the class on a line you can count.
steps.code: val safe = Source( "Safe.kt", """ package movemate import workbench.ksp.annotations.Builder @Builder class Safe private constructor(val code: String) """, ) val run = bench.run(safe, processors = listOf(BuilderProcessorProvider()))

alt.html: JavaFileObject safe = JavaFileObjects.forSourceString("movemate.Safe", """ package movemate; import movemate.annotations.Builder; @Builder public class Safe { private Safe(String code) {} } """); Compilation compilation = javac().withProcessors(new BuilderProcessor()).compile(safe);

steps.say: Write the assertion the user wanted: the error, its text, and line 6, the line of class Safe. Run it and watch it fail with the processor as it is. A test that has never failed hasn't proved anything yet.
steps.code: assertThat(run.exitCode).isEqualTo("COMPILATION_ERROR") assertThat(run.errors).contains( Message('e', "Safe.kt", 6, "SafeBuilder can't call Safe's private constructor. Make the constructor public or internal."), )

alt.html: assertThat(compilation).failed(); assertThat(compilation) .hadErrorContaining("SafeBuilder can't call Safe's private constructor") .inFile(safe) .onLine(6);

steps.say: Fix the processor: the error must be logged on the class symbol, logger.error(message, symbol), not without a node and not on a file. The javac twin passes the element to printMessage.
steps.code: if (constructor.isPrivate()) { logger.error("${name}Builder can't call $name's private constructor. Make the constructor public or internal.", symbol) return null }

alt.html: if (constructor.getModifiers().contains(Modifier.PRIVATE)) { messager.printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, name + "Builder can't call " + name + "'s private constructor. Make the constructor public or internal.", type); return; }

steps.say: Run the test until it passes, and keep it. The bug can't come back without a red test, and the next reader of the suite learns what a private constructor should produce, on which line.

lab.title: A reusable test bench for processors, with golden files
steps: Read GivenProcessors.kt: small copies of lesson 2's card processor and lessons 4 and 5's builder processor, given, so this lesson stands on its own. They are a little shorter than the originals: the setters use apply, and the messages are worded more briefly, so expect @Builder goes on a class where lesson 5 said @Builder needs a class to build. You won't change them; you'll test them.

Read ProcessorBench.kt. Given: Source, the InMemoryCompiler interface, Compiled, Message, newInstance, the three Regex values and GoldenResult. Five functions are yours. Then read KctforkCompiler.kt in src/test: the compiler the tests plug in.

Run the tests: all ten fail with NotImplementedError. This lab is the fifth move, Prove. Each check you build proves one of the other four moves: the messages prove Check, the generated text proves Read and Write, a call into the code proves Write from end to end, and the exit code proves the processor finished.
Write run (trim each source, compile, wrap) and generated (walk the folder; paths with /). Then parseMessage: try the three Regex values in order, and keep only the file name of a path.

Write call, modelled on newInstance: find the method by name and parameter count. A String target is a class name: call a static method with no receiver, or a Kotlin object's method on its INSTANCE field.
Write checkGolden: write the file when it's missing or update is true, and otherwise report the first line that differs, counting from 1.

Prove: run until all ten tests pass. Then change one character in LampBuilder.kt.golden, run the tests and read the failure, and put it back with UPDATE_GOLDEN=true ./gradlew :ksp:test --tests 'workbench.ksp.l08.*'. That run fails once with Wrote the golden file ...; the next run passes.
From memory: close the files and write, on paper, one test for the card processor with all four checks. Then compare it with the drill's answer.
hints: Source.copy(text = text.trimIndent()) keeps the file name. The Compiled from the compiler goes straight into BenchRun(...).
compiled.generatedDir.walk().filter { it.isFile }, then relativeTo(generatedDir).invariantSeparatorsPath gives movemate/LampBuilder.kt on every system.
Regex.matchEntire(line)?.destructured gives the groups. In the KSP pattern the location group is optional, so an empty path means no file and no line.
Modifier.isStatic(method.modifiers) tells a top-level function from an object's method. Wrap the call in unwrapped { ... }, so a test sees the generated code's own exception.
String.lines() keeps a last empty line after a final newline, so a missing last line compares "line two" with "". getOrNull handles files of different lengths.
lab.done: All ten tests in ProcessorBenchTest and BuilderProcessorTest pass, and a one-character change to a golden file fails with its line number.

drill.title: Write the four checks from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Using the bench, write one test for the card processor on @Inventory data class Lamp(val name: String, val bulbs: Int, val shade: String?): check the exit code, check the generated movemate/LampInventoryCard.kt against a golden file, check that there are no messages, and call the card on a lamp with no shade. Then write the compile-testing version of the first three checks for a javac card processor.

answer.html: @Test fun `the card for a lamp with no shade`() { val run = bench.run(lamp, processors = listOf(InventoryProcessorProvider())) assertThat(run.exitCode).isEqualTo("OK") // 1. exit code assertMatchesGolden(run.generated("movemate/LampInventoryCard.kt"), // 2. generated text goldenDir.resolve("LampInventoryCard.kt.golden")) assertThat(run.messages).isEmpty() // 3. messages val lampWithNoShade = run.newInstance("movemate.Lamp", "desk lamp", 1, null) // 4. call the code assertThat(run.call("movemate.LampInventoryCardKt", "inventoryCard", lampWithNoShade)) .isEqualTo("Lamp: name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null") }

alt.title: CardProcessorTest.java
alt.html: // Closest Java equivalent: compile-testing with Truth @Test void theCardForALamp() { Compilation compilation = javac().withProcessors(new CardProcessor()).compile(lamp); assertThat(compilation).succeededWithoutWarnings(); // 1 and 3 assertThat(compilation).generatedSourceFile("movemate.LampInventoryCard") .hasSourceEquivalentTo(JavaFileObjects.forResource("golden/LampInventoryCard.java")); // 2 // 4: call the card from a test in a module whose build runs the processor }

recap: A processor test compiles a few lines in memory: kctfork runs KSP2 and the Kotlin compiler in the test's JVM, as compile-testing runs javac. The processor is passed directly, so the services file plays no part.

The four checks are the exit code, the generated text, the messages by file and line, and a call into the generated code through the result's class loader. The first two alone passed a builder that had lost a question mark.

A golden file stores the expected output and reports the first differing line. Write a missing one and review it once, rewrite on purpose with UPDATE_GOLDEN=true, and pair it with a call into the code, because formatting changes fail it too.
Error tests pin the text and the line: KSP and javac report the declaration's line, counted from the package line once the indent is trimmed. Never compare paths; they point into a temporary folder.

The limit: an in-memory test runs a fresh, clean build every time, so it can't see wrong Dependencies, a broken services file or untracked options. Those need a real build, by hand in the playground or with Gradle TestKit.

explain.prompt: A teammate's processor tests all look like this: compile a class, assert the exit code is OK, assert the output contains the class name. They say the processor is well tested. Explain what those tests prove, what they miss, and what you would add.
explain.answer: Those tests prove that the processor ran without crashing on the inputs they use, and that it wrote a file with the right name in it. They miss almost every real bug, because generated code can compile and still be wrong: a builder that drops a question mark from shade: String? passes both checks and fails the first time someone passes null. I'd add the other two checks. First, call the generated code through the result's class loader, with the awkward values: a null, an empty list, a missing required field. Second, test the refusals: give the processor an interface or a private constructor, and assert the exit code, the message text and the file and line, which is the declaration's line. Golden files help too, as long as each one sits next to a call into the code, because formatting changes fail them. And I'd say plainly what in-memory tests can't see: incremental builds and the services file need a real build, in a playground or with Gradle TestKit.

deeper.html:
The bench splits the compiler from the checks, and the same idea works inside a processor. Split it in two: one half turns KS symbols into a plain data model (the class name, the parameters and their types), the other turns that model into a FileSpec. The second half can then be tested with fileSpec.toString() and no compiler at all, in milliseconds, and the compile tests shrink to a few that check the wiring.

A few kctfork details are worth knowing before you read older blog posts. Since version 0.10.0 it supports KSP2 only, and configureKsp(useKsp2 = true) no longer compiles: write configureKsp { symbolProcessorProviders += ... }. Setting providers before KSP is configured throws IllegalStateException: KSP not configured, which is exactly what the README's snippet does. kspWithCompilation does nothing on KSP2. kctfork compiles with its own Kotlin compiler, 2.4.20 in version 0.14.0, while this course builds with 2.4.21, and it was built against KSP 2.3.12, which is why the lab's build pins every KSP artifact to 2.3.14. Without that pin, any source with a property fails with a NoSuchMethodError.

On the Java side, compile-testing's documented examples live in its package-info.java, and its checks cover the outcome (succeeded(), failed()), the messages (hadErrorContaining(...).inFile(...).onLine(...), also atColumn and onLineContaining) and the generated files (generatedSourceFile(...), hasSourceEquivalentTo(...)). It passes processors to javac directly, so JDK 23's change, which stopped javac from running processors it merely finds on the class path, doesn't affect it.
